title: Leaching poisonous plant foods

names.note: Anderson (1996) records jinali as the flat grinding rocks beside creeks at zamia-processing sites.

identification.basis: The dictionary gives ngabal 'soak, leach' and describes at least ten foods (zamia, scrub zamia, hairy yam, biyangkal, bujabay, two wild plums, two mangrove fruits, kajimarra flour) as needing to be leached, soaked or washed before eating. Roth (1901) and Anderson (1996) describe the Bloomfield River methods in detail.

summary:
**Leaching** is how Kuku Yalanji people made poisonous plant foods safe to eat. The food was cooked, broken down very fine, sifted, and then washed in running water or in bark troughs of fresh water until the bitter taste, which is the poison, was gone. The dictionary's word is **[ngabal](word:ngabal)** 'soak, leach' [ref:hershberger1982]. It was used for [zamia](entry:zamia), [black bean](entry:black-bean), the hairy [yam](entry:yam), *[bujabay](word:bujabay)*, [wild plums](entry:wild-plums) and [mangrove](entry:mangroves) fruits [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1901].

**Safety first: these foods are poisonous until properly prepared.** A short cut, such as coarse meal, too little water, still water or too short a time, can leave enough poison to make someone very sick. This page records how it was done. It is not a recipe to try from a book.

infobox.label: Containers

sections.heading: Names
sections.body:
**[Ngabal](word:ngabal)** is 'soak, leach' and **[julurril](word:julurril)** is 'to wash something'. **[Nyurrbal](word:nyurrbal)** is 'to grind, sharpen', and meal ground properly is **[dirka](word:dirka)** 'fine, finely ground'. The taste that leaching removes is **[marrbal](word:marrbal)** 'sour, bitter taste', and **[kuli](word:kuli)** means 'poison' as well as 'anger' and 'trouble' [ref:hershberger1982]. Anderson recorded **[jinali](word:jinali)**, the dictionary's 'smooth rock', as the name of the flat creek-side grinding rocks with small hollows that were used every year at [zamia](entry:zamia) camps [ref:anderson1996] [ref:hershberger1982].

The dictionary marks many foods as needing this treatment. **[Marra](word:marra)**, the zamia nut, is 'roasted, ground and leached to make flour'. **[Julbin](word:julbin)**, the scrub zamia, is 'edible when ground and leached with water'. **[Wukay](word:wukay)**, the hairy yam, 'must be cooked, ground and leached before eating'. **[Biyangkal](word:biyangkal)** must be 'leached for a couple hours in many changes of water'. The fruit of **[bujabay](word:bujabay)** 'must be leached (in water)'. **[Junda](word:junda)** and **[jundul](word:jundul)** are wild plums that are poisonous unless leached. The fruit of the mangroves **[kajul](word:kajul)** and **[kakaji](word:kakaji)** must be soaked or leached [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Description
sections.body:
Every recorded method has the same four stages:

1. **Cook** the food by roasting, baking in the ashes or an [earth oven](entry:earth-oven), or steaming.
2. **Break it down** by pounding, grinding, mashing, or cutting it into very fine chips or slices.
3. **Sift or strain** it through a [dilly bag](entry:dilly-bags).
4. **Wash it** in running water, or in fresh water that is changed again and again.

The fineness matters. On the lower Tully River, [black bean](entry:black-bean) that was 'not sliced up very fine' kept its bitter taste [ref:roth1901]. So does the water. A creek or a steady trickle keeps carrying the poison away. In a trough, the water has to be poured off and replaced many times.

sections.heading: Where it was done
sections.body: Leaching was done beside water: a small, fast creek, or [bark troughs](entry:bark-troughs) filled and emptied again and again [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1901]. On the coast, [mangrove](entry:mangroves) food was finished in basin-shaped holes in the sand, 'often to be noticed along the coast-line' near the mangrove swamps [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: Food by food
sections.body:
- **Zamia (marra), Bloomfield.** Roast the nuts and crack them. Keep the kernels four or five days, then pound or grind them to flour. Sift through a palm-fibre bag. Put the flour in a grass bag folded into a basin beside a stream, and lead water into it along a channel of leaves so that it percolates 'right through the night'. Ready by morning, it keeps three or four days but no longer [ref:roth1901] [ref:anderson1996]. The dictionary records another way, **[kajimarra](word:kajimarra)**: the food is 'rolled in junjun leaves and left in water for several weeks, then ground and roasted' [ref:hershberger1982].
- **[Black bean](entry:black-bean) (baway).** On the Bloomfield it was baked, pounded, sifted and washed in a [bark trough](entry:bark-troughs) like the [yam](entry:yam) [ref:roth1901] [ref:anderson1996]. At Atherton it was baked from sunrise to midday, cut into very fine chips and left overnight in a [lawyer-cane](entry:lawyer-cane) bag in a running creek. On the lower Tully it was steamed, sliced very fine and left in bags in a stream for 'quite a couple of days' [ref:roth1901].
- **Hairy yam (wukay).** Bake about four hours, mash in a palm-fibre bag over a bark trough, and strain. Then fill the trough, let it settle and pour off the water, 'seven or eight waters' in all. Eat it the same day [ref:roth1901] [ref:anderson1996]. **[Biyangkal](word:biyangkal)** needs 'a couple hours in many changes of water' [ref:hershberger1982].
- **Bujabay.** Anderson identifies it as *Endiandra palmerstonii*, Queensland walnut: roasted on the fire, pounded, sifted in a [dilly bag](entry:dilly-bags) and leached [ref:anderson1996].
- **Wild plums (junda, jundul).** The sources disagree. The dictionary says junda 'is poisonous and must be leached before eating' [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth's Bloomfield *[junda](word:junda)* (*Pygeum turnerianum*, in season January to March) was pounded whole, sifted through a palm bag, kneaded into cakes, wrapped in [wild-ginger](entry:wild-ginger) leaves and baked in the ashes [ref:roth1901]. Anderson's table marks it as not leached [ref:anderson1996]. Jundul is not identified.
- **Mangrove fruits (kajul, kakaji).** Neither species is identified. Roth's entries for neighbouring mangroves, which carry Guugu Yimithirr names from Cooktown and Cape Bedford, show the methods. *Avicennia* fruit was baked, then washed in a sieve-bag. The long seedlings of *Bruguiera* were baked, pounded, skinned and washed four or five times in a bark trough, then drained in a sand hole. On the lower Tully, *Bruguiera gymnorrhiza* was baked, sliced and soaked all night [ref:roth1901].

sections.heading: How it was done: the Bloomfield trough method
sections.body:
This is the hairy-yam method, the fullest Kuku Yalanji account (Roth from R. Hislop [ref:roth1901]; Anderson from Kuku Yalanji teachers [ref:anderson1996]):

1. **Go to a small, fast creek** with the food, a palm-fibre [dilly bag](entry:dilly-bags) and [bark troughs](entry:bark-troughs).
2. **Clean the food**, removing dirt and roots.
3. **Cook it** in a stone [earth oven](entry:earth-oven) for about four hours, until soft, and let it cool.
4. **Mash it by hand inside the bag**, holding the bag over a bark trough. Pour water through, mash again and strain, until only fibre and skin are left in the bag. Throw that away.
5. **Fill the trough with water**, stir, and let it stand about half an hour until the food settles and the water clears.
6. **Watch for the oily film.** 'Within a short time, an oily substance appeared on top of the water. This was said to be the ‘poison’' [ref:anderson1996]. Pour it off with the water.
7. **Add fresh water and repeat**, for several hours, 'until the water was completely free of the oil and any bitter taste gone' [ref:anderson1996]. Roth says it can take seven or eight waters [ref:roth1901].
8. **Drain it** in a hole about a metre across, lined with clean white sand, with a rolled leaf in the bottom to carry the water away [ref:anderson1996].
9. **Eat it that day.** It ferments quickly [ref:roth1901].

**Containers.** The palm-fibre bag has the finest mesh and was the sieve. The grass bag, folded into a basin, was the colander for running water [ref:roth1901]. Bark troughs, the dictionary's **[dubal](word:dubal)** 'coolamon' (Roth's Bloomfield *tu-bal*), were made of eucalypt or other bark [ref:roth1904] [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:anderson1996]. Leaves of [pandanus](entry:pandanus) or [wild ginger](entry:wild-ginger) made a trough to lead water into the bag [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
- **Raw means poisonous.** The dictionary calls junda and kakaji poisonous until leached, and Anderson calls the hairy [yam](entry:yam) 'otherwise toxic' [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:anderson1996].
- **The oily-film and bitterness checks are traditional signs, not laboratory tests.** They were used by experienced people who knew each plant. Do not rely on taste alone, and never feed experimental batches to children.
- **Each food has its own method.** Some yams need only roasting, others hours of washing [ref:anderson1996]. Mistaking one plant for another is the main danger.
- **Prepared food spoils.** Yam mash ferments within the day, and [zamia](entry:zamia) flour keeps only three or four days [ref:roth1901].
- **Smoke can poison too.** The smoke from roasting **[jinjay](word:jinjay)** nuts is poisonous [ref:hershberger1982].

Learn these methods hands-on from Traditional Owners who still hold them.

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: Old processing places and grinding stones are cultural heritage, and Queensland law gives everyone a duty of care not to harm Aboriginal cultural heritage [ref:acha2003]. Native title holders' gathering for personal, domestic or non-commercial communal needs is protected from licence and permit requirements by section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993* [ref:alrc]. Where and how each food was treated differs from place to place: see each place above.

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: **[Nyangarril](word:nyangarril)** 'pour, spill'; **[dindal](word:dindal)** 'to roast on coals'; **[kurrma](word:kurrma)** 'earth oven'; **[banjay](word:banjay)**, a small round wild yam 'roasted in the fire, ground up and eaten'; **[balja](word:balja)**, 'a kind of food. It is cooked in the fire, ground up and eaten' [ref:hershberger1982].

locations.summary: **Leaching was done in this country.** About 1900 Walter Roth watched yams and *Tacca* tubers washed through bags and troughs on the **Morehead and Musgrave rivers**, in the Princess Charlotte Bay country the Hann drains into [ref:roth1901] [ref:qpws-rinyirru-culture]. The Thaypan native title area takes in Musgrave station and the upper Morehead [ref:fca-thaypan]. These are Roth's words about what he saw; the people of this country hold the knowledge of how it is done.

sections.heading: Where the foods grow here
sections.body: The Kuku Thaypan Elders describe their mixed-tree country, on slightly raised light sandy soil, as having 'a diverse understory of brachychiton and yams', and they protect yams with 'a cool fire that has burnt the dead grass around the yams' [ref:standley2019]. A Thaypan man named among his country's foods 'lady apples, white apples, bally yams that grow on a long stem, bush carrot and bush potato' [ref:fca-thaypan]. The Atlas of Living Australia holds no zamia (*Cycas*) records, two *Tacca* records and one *Dioscorea* yam record in a box of about 90 × 85 km around the middle Hann, Laura and western Rinyirru [ref:ala-hann]. So the [zamia](entry:zamia) method on this page is not recorded from here.

sections.heading: How it was done here
sections.body:
**Hairy yam, Morehead River** (Roth's *Dioscorea sativa* var. *rotunda*; Koko-rarmul *rau-ola*) [ref:roth1901]:

1. Cut the roots 'into halves or quarters, and washed in a bark trough'.
2. Bake them 'in a hot ant-bed covered with tea-tree bark and earth' for about twenty minutes, until soft.
3. Put them in a grass [dilly bag](entry:dilly-bags) and squeeze it under water in a trough, so 'the mealy substance' passes through the bag. Throw away what is left in the bag.
4. Let the meal settle, pour off the water with the scum, pour on fresh water, 'and so on for some four or five times'.
5. Hollow a round basin in the sand with a piece of bark resting down its side. Pour the watery meal onto the bark so it runs gently into the hole and the water drains away.
6. 'As soon as fairly dry it is eaten.'

**Tacca tubers, Morehead and Musgrave rivers** [ref:roth1901]:

1. Rub the tubers on 'a rough stick ... (acting after the method of a "nutmeg-grater")' into a bark trough of water.
2. Squeeze the mixture through 'a "sieve" formed of an infolded dilly-bag' into fresh water in another trough.
3. Let it settle, 'for which some time is required', then wash it 'once or twice' and let the water run off.
4. Scrape up the sediment with a shell and cook it 'in hot ashes like a "damper"'.

sections.heading: Safety here
sections.body: Roth wrote down the steps, not the knowledge of which plants and which parts are safe. Don't try these from a page; learn them from the Traditional Owners.

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: In Rinyirru (Lakefield) National Park: 'Do not remove plant material, living or dead' [ref:qpws-rinyirru-about]. The native title determinations of November 2023 recognise the Possum People's rights on the upper Hann and the Thaypan people's on the middle and lower Hann, including the right to take the natural resources of their country [ref:fca-possum] [ref:fca-thaypan].

locations.summary: On the Western Yalanji side the zamia grows north of Mount Carbine but has not been recorded near [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) [ref:ala-cycas-north] [ref:ala-fibre]. Western Yalanji people hold the knowledge of which foods were treated on this country.

sections.heading: Where the foods grow here
sections.body: The zamia *Cycas media* has been collected in the dry country about 25 km north of Mount Carbine [ref:ala-cycas-north], but the Atlas holds no *Cycas* records within 30 km of [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) [ref:ala-fibre]. Edward Palmer recorded a related technique from the Mitchell, Lynd and Pennefather rivers. *Typhonium* tubers were 'roasted and broken with a stone, pounded a good deal, and roasted several times before using', with no washing [ref:roth1901]. Western Yalanji people hold the knowledge of which foods were treated on this country.

locations.summary: The fullest Kuku Yalanji accounts of leaching come from the Bloomfield River, from Roth's informant R. Hislop and from Anderson's Kuku Yalanji teachers [ref:roth1901] [ref:anderson1996]. The methods in the general sections of this page are theirs.

sections.heading: Where it was done here
sections.body: The Bloomfield [zamia](entry:zamia) camps were set up 'ideally beside a shallow, but fast-flowing section of creek' next to the jinali grinding rocks. In the [dry season](entry:seasons) these camps could hold up to 100 people, the women processing while the young men brought in meat and honey [ref:anderson1996]. [Yams](entry:yam) were taken 'near a small, rapid creek' [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Seasons here
sections.body: On the Bloomfield, [zamia](entry:zamia) was 'fit to eat from July to January' [ref:roth1901], and Anderson puts the big processing camps in the mid to late [dry season](entry:seasons) [ref:anderson1996]. The hairy [yam](entry:yam) was the main food from about mid-February to mid-May, the wet season [ref:roth1901]. Nuts could be stored for up to two months. In the wet, that meant fewer trips away from camp in heavy rain and flood [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: In 1982 Bloomfield women still processed hairy [yam](entry:yam) in bush camps. They boiled it in empty metal flour drums and separated the poison in plastic buckets, but still did the first mashing in palm-fibre [dilly bags](entry:dilly-bags) [ref:anderson1996]. The jinali grinding stones were still in place at several sites, though unused for thirty or forty years [ref:anderson1996].
